newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-FURIOUS BIDDING AS SILKS ARE SOLD.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-FURIOUS BIDDING AS SILKS ARE SOLD.

text.p: Horse racing fans spent almost 130,000 pounds ($214,700) on Wednesday buying the racing colours that took their fancy.
Bidding was fast and furious at the first ever auction of racing colours in the sales room of Sotheby's, whose staff obligingly modelled the 12 elegant silks.
In racing, one-colour silks are highly prized by owners eager for their charges to stand out from the equine crowd.
The chance to run a future champion in dark blue silks provoked the most spirited tussle with a telephone bidder finally paying 28,750 pounds ($46,000).
Terracotta, lime green and cerise were the other single colours that had the bidding at fever pitch.

Peter Mines, managing director of a London stationery company, happily paid almost 10,000 pounds ($16,000) for a gold and black combinatioon which he hopes to see triumphant in the country's top steeplechases.
"Our company is celebrating its 50th anniversary next year. We felt this was well worth it for advertising purposes. I didn't get carried away," he said after the sale.

The British Horse Racing Board was delighted with its gamble on going public with the sale of colours for the first time. "It has vindicated our decision. The prices were in excess of our expectations," a spokesman said.
Sotheby's were equally delighted by the decision to stage their first horse racing memorabilia sale in which the 337 lots raised almost 1.8 million pounds ($2.88 million).

Among the more exotic items up for sale was the telegram of sympathy sent to jockey Herbert Jones after his horse was brought down by a suffragette who was killed when she ran out on the Epsom Derby track.

The 1913 telegram, which sold for 2,415 pounds ($3,860) to a private London buyer, read: "Queen Alexandra was very sorry indeed to aread of your sad accident caused through the abominable conduct of a brutal lunatic woman."
Among the last lots sold were the racing silks worn by Lester Piggott as he steered Never Say Die to victory in the 1954 Epsom Derby when he was just 18 years old.
They sold for 5,520 pounds ($8,830) to an overseas collector phoning in a bid.
Willie Carson, recovering from a horrific riding accident last summer, was tempted by some of the memorabilia.
But when asked if he might bid for the silks of his arch rival Piggott, the Scotsman was quick to reply with feeling: "No, I will not."

Veteran BBC television commentator Peter O'Sullevan, known as the voice of British racing, said of the packed sales room: "It is a fantastic tribute to the sport and the way it captures the imagination.
"There is nothing more beautiful than a thoroughbred. Horses inspire so many people."
